scenes.script: The Fermi Paradox describes a simple contradiction. If life is possible on Earth, it should be possible on many other planets. The Milky Way has hundreds of billions of stars. Many have planets. Some are rocky. Some sit in stable orbits. And the galaxy is old, much older than human civilization. If intelligent life happens often, some civilizations should be millions of years ahead of us. A million-year head start is enough to send probes, signals, or machines across huge distances. They do not need faster-than-light travel. Slow expansion is enough over galactic time. So we should expect evidence somewhere: a signal, a probe, a changed star, a megastructure, something. But so far, there is no confirmed signal from another civilization. No confirmed alien probe. No confirmed megastructure. That is the paradox: the numbers make the galaxy look crowded, but the evidence says silence. So one assumption is wrong. Maybe life is extremely rare. Maybe simple life is common, but intelligence is rare. Maybe technological civilizations destroy themselves, go quiet, or leave traces we do not recognize. Or maybe our search is still too small. The Fermi Paradox is not proof that we are alone. It is proof that one of our easy guesses about life in the galaxy is probably wrong.
